questions.q: One root of x² − (2 + i)x + (1 + i) = 0 is 1. What is the other root?
questions.x: The sum of the roots is 2 + i, so the other root is (2 + i) − 1 = 1 + i. Check with the product: 1 × (1 + i) = 1 + i, the constant term. The coefficients are not real, so the conjugate 1 − i need not be a root.

questions.q: The function f: Z → Z is defined by f(x) = 2x + 1. Which statement is true?
o: f is onto but not one-one
f is both one-one and onto
f is one-one but not onto
f is neither one-one nor onto
questions.x: 2a + 1 = 2b + 1 gives a = b, so f is one-one. But f(x) is always odd, so an even integer such as 2 is never an image: f is not onto Z. (As a function on R the same rule would be a bijection.)

questions.q: The graph of y = a·2ˣ + b passes through (0, 3) and (1, 5). What is the value of y at x = 2?
questions.x: a + b = 3 and 2a + b = 5 give a = 2 and b = 1, so y = 2·2ˣ + 1 and y(2) = 8 + 1 = 9. Continuing in equal steps 3, 5, 7 wrongly treats the graph as a straight line.

questions.q: For x > 0, at which x does the graph of y = 2 sin(x − π/3) first reach its maximum value?
questions.x: The maximum value 2 needs x − π/3 = π/2 (the next earlier one, −3π/2, gives x < 0), so x = π/2 + π/3 = 5π/6. The graph is 2 sin x shifted π/3 to the right; shifting left gives π/6.

questions.q: lim(x→∞) x sin(1/x) equals:
questions.x: Put t = 1/x; as x → ∞, t → 0⁺ and x sin(1/x) = (sin t)/t → 1. Compare (sin x)/x as x → ∞, which tends to 0.

questions.q: What is the value of the determinant |[[101, 102], [103, 104]]|?
questions.x: Subtract row 1 from row 2 (the value does not change): |[[101, 102], [2, 2]]| = 202 − 204 = −2. Direct check: 101 × 104 − 102 × 103 = 10504 − 10506 = −2.

questions.q: The line y = x + 1 meets the curve y = x² − 1 at two points. What is the distance between these points?
questions.x: x² − 1 = x + 1 gives x² − x − 2 = 0, so x = 2 or x = −1 and the points are (2, 3) and (−1, 0). Distance = √(3² + 3²) = 3√2. Using only the difference in x gives 3.

questions.q: ω is a complex cube root of unity. Which quadratic equation has roots 2ω and 2ω²?
questions.x: Sum = 2(ω + ω²) = 2(−1) = −2 and product = 4ω³ = 4, so x² − (−2)x + 4 = x² + 2x + 4 = 0. Check: its discriminant 4 − 16 = −12 gives roots −1 ± √3 i, which are 2ω and 2ω². x² + x + 1 = 0 has roots ω and ω², without the factor 2.

questions.q: In an infinite G.P. with positive terms, every term is twice the sum of all the terms that follow it. What is the common ratio?
questions.x: The terms after a are ar, ar², …, with sum ar/(1 − r). So a = 2ar/(1 − r), giving 1 − r = 2r and r = 1/3. Check with 1, 1/3, 1/9, …: the terms after 1 sum to (1/3)/(2/3) = 1/2, and twice that is 1.

questions.q: What is the harmonic mean of the roots of x² − 10x + 16 = 0?
questions.x: For roots α, β the harmonic mean is 2αβ/(α + β) = 2 × 16/10 = 16/5. Check: the roots are 2 and 8, and 2 × 2 × 8/10 = 3.2. 5 is their arithmetic mean and 4 their geometric mean.

questions.q: If P(n, 3) = 210, what is the value of n?
For |x| < 1, the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + x)²/(1 − x) is:
questions.x: (1 + 2x + x²)(1 + x + x² + …): the x² terms are 1·x² + 2x·x + x²·1, so the coefficient is 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. Missing the cross term 2x·x gives 2.

questions.q: If 3 sin θ + 4 cos θ = 5, what is the value of tan θ?
questions.x: Put 4 cos θ = 5 − 3 sin θ and square: 16(1 − sin²θ) = 25 − 30 sin θ + 9 sin²θ, so 25 sin²θ − 30 sin θ + 9 = 0, i.e. (5 sin θ − 3)² = 0. Then sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5 and tan θ = 3/4. 4/3 swaps sine and cosine.

questions.q: For every θ, cos θ − sin θ equals:
questions.x: √2 cos(θ + π/4) = √2(cos θ · √2/2 − sin θ · √2/2) = cos θ − sin θ. Both √2 cos(θ − π/4) and √2 sin(θ + π/4) expand to cos θ + sin θ.

questions.q: For every θ, sin 3θ equals:
questions.x: sin 3θ = sin(2θ + θ) = 2 sin θ cos²θ + (1 − 2 sin²θ) sin θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ. Check θ = 90°: sin 270° = −1 and 3 − 4 = −1. The form 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ belongs to cos 3θ.

questions.q: On the interval [0, 2π], at how many points do the graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x meet?
questions.x: They meet where tan x = 1, that is at x = π/4 and x = 5π/4 in [0, 2π]. At x = 5π/4 both values are −√2/2, so this second point is easy to miss.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, b = 6, c = 10, A is obtuse and the area is 15√3. What is a?
questions.x: ½ × 6 × 10 × sin A = 15√3 gives sin A = √3/2, and A is obtuse, so A = 120°. Then a² = 36 + 100 − 120 cos 120° = 196 and a = 14. Taking A = 60° gives a = 2√19.

questions.q: For which of these values of x is sin⁻¹(sin x) = x true?
questions.x: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only when x lies in the principal range [−π/2, π/2], and only π/3 does. For example sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) = sin⁻¹(√3/2) = π/3, not 2π/3.

questions.q: If y = eˣ sin x, then y″ − 2y′ + 2y equals:
questions.x: y′ = eˣ(sin x + cos x) and y″ = eˣ(sin x + cos x + cos x − sin x) = 2eˣ cos x. Then y″ − 2y′ + 2y = 2eˣ cos x − 2eˣ sin x − 2eˣ cos x + 2eˣ sin x = 0.

questions.q: The radius of a circular ink blot grows at 0.5 cm/s. How fast is its area growing when the radius is 4 cm?
questions.x: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr × dr/dt = 2π × 4 × 0.5 = 4π cm²/s. Forgetting dr/dt gives 8π, and πr² gives 16π (the area itself).

questions.q: If y = x^(ln x) (x > 0), what is dy/dx at x = e?
questions.x: Take logs: ln y = (ln x)², so y′/y = 2 ln x/x. At x = e, y = e¹ = e and y′ = e × 2/e = 2. Treating ln x as a constant power gives (ln x)x^(ln x − 1) = 1 at x = e.

questions.q: ∫ x/√(1 − x²) dx, for |x| < 1, equals:
questions.x: Put u = 1 − x², du = −2x dx: the integral is −½∫u^(−1/2) du = −u^(1/2) + C = −√(1 − x²) + C. Check: d/dx[−(1 − x²)^(1/2)] = x/√(1 − x²).

questions.q: The area of the region between the curve y = x² − 2x and the x-axis is:
questions.x: The curve meets the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 2 and lies below it in between, so the area is ∫₀² (2x − x²) dx = 4 − 8/3 = 4/3. Integrating x² − 2x directly gives −4/3, but an area is never negative.

questions.q: Water drains from a tank so that the depth h falls at a rate proportional to √h. With k a positive constant, which equation models this?
questions.x: The rate dh/dt is proportional to √h, and it is negative because the depth falls: dh/dt = −k√h. Without the minus sign the depth would rise.

questions.q: Which of these lines is farthest from the origin?
questions.x: Distances from O: 12/5 = 2.4, 3/√2 ≈ 2.12, 26/13 = 2 and 5/√5 = √5 ≈ 2.24. The largest is 2.4, for 3x + 4y = 12.

questions.q: Minimise z = x + 2y subject to 2x + y ≥ 6, x + y ≥ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. What is the minimum value of z?
questions.x: The region is unbounded with corners (0, 6), (2, 2) and (4, 0), where z = 12, 6 and 4. Moving further along the x-axis only increases z, so the minimum is 4 at (4, 0). Stopping at the crossing point (2, 2) gives 6.

questions.q: What is the area of the triangle formed by the vertex of the parabola y² = 8x and the two ends of its latus rectum?
questions.x: 4a = 8 gives a = 2, so the ends of the latus rectum are (2, 4) and (2, −4). The triangle has base 8 and height 2, so its area is ½ × 8 × 2 = 8.

questions.q: What are the centre and the length of the major axis of the ellipse 4x² + 9y² − 16x + 18y − 11 = 0?
questions.x: Complete the squares: 4(x − 2)² − 16 + 9(y + 1)² − 9 = 11, so 4(x − 2)² + 9(y + 1)² = 36, i.e. (x − 2)²/9 + (y + 1)²/4 = 1. Centre (2, −1), a = 3, major axis 2a = 6.

questions.q: A particle has position r(t) = 2t i + t² j + 3k. What is its acceleration?
questions.x: r′(t) = 2i + 2tj and r″(t) = 2j, a constant. 2i + 2tj is the velocity, not the acceleration.

questions.q: Newton–Raphson is applied to f(x) = x³ − 4x − 1 with x₀ = 2. What is x₁?
questions.x: f(2) = 8 − 8 − 1 = −1 and f′(x) = 3x² − 4 gives f′(2) = 8, so x₁ = 2 − (−1)/8 = 2.125. Getting the sign wrong gives 1.875.

questions.q: A piece 12.3 ± 0.1 cm long is cut from a rod 20.5 ± 0.2 cm long. The length left over, with its uncertainty, is:
questions.x: 20.5 − 12.3 = 8.2 cm, and when quantities are subtracted their absolute uncertainties still add: 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3 cm. Subtracting the uncertainties as well gives the tempting ± 0.1 cm.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 0.3 m on a fixed axle has a tangential force of 20 N at its rim turning it clockwise and a tangential force of 30 N on its hub, 0.1 m from the axle, turning it anticlockwise. The net torque on the wheel is:
questions.x: Clockwise torque = 20 × 0.3 = 6 N m; anticlockwise torque = 30 × 0.1 = 3 N m; net = 3 N m clockwise. Thinking the bigger force wins gives anticlockwise; adding the torques gives 9 N m.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward and reaches a greatest height of 45 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed when it is at half this height on the way up is:
questions.x: Launch speed: u² = 2gH = 900, so u = 30 m s⁻¹. At 22.5 m: v² = 900 − 2 × 10 × 22.5 = 450, so v = 15√2 m s⁻¹. Check by energy: half the kinetic energy is left, so v = u/√2. Halving the speed gives the tempting 15 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A horizontal jet of water strikes a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and stops without bouncing back. 2 kg of water hits the wall every second. The force of the water on the wall is:
questions.x: F = rate of change of momentum = (mass per second) × change in velocity = 2 × 10 = 20 N. 40 N would need the water to rebound at 10 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the distance a body falls from rest in the first 2 s is:
questions.x: s = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m. Forgetting the ½ gives 40 m; forgetting to square t gives 10 m.

questions.q: A force F does work on a body while it moves a distance d, the force making 60° with the displacement (cos 60° = 0.5). If instead a force 2F acts along the displacement over the same distance d, the work done becomes:
questions.x: W₁ = Fd cos 60° = 0.5Fd and W₂ = 2Fd cos 0° = 2Fd, so W₂/W₁ = 4. Doubling the force alone, without the change from cos 60° to cos 0°, gives the tempting twice as large.

questions.q: The SI unit of angular momentum is:
questions.x: L = Iω, with I in kg m² and ω in s⁻¹ (radian is dimensionless), so L is in kg m² s⁻¹ (= J s). kg m s⁻¹ is linear momentum and kg m² is moment of inertia.

questions.q: A balloon holds 10 m³ of helium (density 0.2 kg m⁻³) in air of density 1.3 kg m⁻³. Ignoring the mass of the balloon fabric, the largest load it can hold up is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: Upthrust = 1.3 × 10 × 10 = 130 N; weight of helium = 0.2 × 10 × 10 = 20 N; spare lift = 110 N, which supports a mass of 110/10 = 11 kg. Ignoring the helium's weight gives 13 kg; giving the 110 N as kg gives 110 kg.

questions.q: At the instant when a particle in SHM moves at half its maximum speed, what fraction of its total energy is potential energy?
questions.x: KE ∝ v², so at half the maximum speed KE = ¼ of the total energy; the rest, 3/4, is potential energy. 1/4 is the kinetic share, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: An oscillating system is displaced and left to vibrate on its own, with no damping and no driving force. It vibrates:
o: At its natural frequency with steadily falling amplitude
At a frequency that steadily falls
At its natural frequency with constant amplitude
questions.x: These are free oscillations: the system vibrates at its own natural frequency, and with no damping no energy is lost, so the amplitude stays constant. A falling amplitude would mean damping.

questions.q: Two tuning forks of 340 Hz and 345 Hz are sounded together. The time between two successive loud sounds (waxings) is:
questions.x: Beat frequency = 345 − 340 = 5 Hz, so there are 5 loud sounds per second, one every 1/5 = 0.2 s. Giving the beat frequency 5 as a time is the usual slip.

questions.q: Gravitational-wave observatories use two or more interferometers placed thousands of kilometres apart. A main reason is that:
o: A real wave shows up in all of them within milliseconds, while local shaking affects only one
The waves can be detected only at night at any one site
Each interferometer measures a different speed for the wave
One detector must send its laser beam to the other
questions.x: Local disturbances such as traffic or small earthquakes shake one site only, but a gravitational wave travelling at the speed of light reaches detectors 3000 km apart within about 10 ms. Matching signals at both sites confirm a real event, and the time difference helps locate the source.

questions.q: A tiny lamp acts as a point source of light in a uniform medium. The wavefronts spreading out from it are:
o: Cylindrical, with the lamp on their axis
Parabolic, with the lamp at the focus
questions.x: From a point source the light spreads equally in all directions at the same speed, so the points in the same phase lie on spheres centred on the source. Plane wavefronts arise only very far from the source, and cylindrical ones come from a line source such as a slit.

questions.q: A Carnot engine has an efficiency of 1/3. When its sink temperature is lowered by 50 K, with the source unchanged, its efficiency becomes 1/2. What is the source temperature?
Hydrogen and oxygen are kept at the same temperature. The ratio of the average translational kinetic energy of a hydrogen molecule to that of an oxygen molecule is:
questions.x: The average translational kinetic energy is (3/2)kT, which depends only on temperature, not on the mass of the molecule. So the ratio is 1; the factor 4 is the ratio of rms speeds, not of energies.

questions.q: For a capacitor being charged, a graph of potential difference V (vertical axis) against charge Q (horizontal axis) is a straight line through the origin. The area under this graph gives the:
questions.x: The work to add charge dQ at potential V is V dQ, so the area under the V-Q graph is the energy stored, ½QV. The slope of the graph is 1/C.

questions.q: The separation between the plates of a parallel-plate air capacitor is doubled, with the plate area unchanged. Its capacitance:
questions.x: C = ε₀A/d, so C is inversely proportional to the separation: doubling d halves C.

questions.q: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor in series, the 2 Ω resistor being joined to the positive terminal. Taking the negative terminal as 0 V, the potential of the junction between the two resistors is:
questions.x: I = 12/6 = 2 A. Going from the positive terminal (12 V) through the 2 Ω resistor, the potential falls by 2 × 2 = 4 V, leaving 8 V; this is also the 8 V across the 4 Ω resistor. Taking the drop itself as the answer gives 4 V.

questions.q: A carbon resistor has colour bands red, red, brown and gold, in that order. Its actual resistance can lie anywhere between:
questions.x: Red = 2, red = 2, brown multiplier = 10¹, so R = 22 × 10 = 220 Ω; gold means ±5%, which is ±11 Ω, giving 209 Ω to 231 Ω. Taking gold as ±10% gives 198-242 Ω; reading brown as two zeros gives 2090-2310 Ω.

questions.q: On the resistance scale of an ohmmeter (in an AVO meter), the zero-ohm mark is at the full-scale-deflection end of the scale because:
o: The meter's internal cell is disconnected when the probes are joined
A zero resistance draws no current from the cell
With the probes joined directly, the circuit has least resistance and the largest current flows
The pointer spring is weakest at full scale
questions.x: The ohmmeter uses its own cell. With zero external resistance the current is largest, so the needle is set to full scale there and marked 0 Ω; larger resistances give smaller currents, so the scale runs backwards and is non-linear.

questions.q: An electron moves horizontally towards the east through a uniform magnetic field that points vertically downward. The direction of the magnetic force on the electron is:
questions.x: For a positive charge F is along v × B: east × downward points north. The electron's charge is negative, so its force is the opposite way: south. Forgetting the negative charge gives north.

questions.q: The coil of an AC generator is made to rotate twice as fast in the same field. The peak emf and the frequency of the output, respectively:
questions.x: ε₀ = NABω, so doubling ω doubles the peak emf, and f = ω/2π also doubles. Speed changes both, not just the frequency.

questions.q: In a three-phase supply, the voltage between any one line and the neutral is 220 V. The voltage between any two of the lines is about (√3 ≈ 1.73):
questions.x: The two line voltages are 120° apart, so the p.d. between them is √3 times the phase voltage: 1.73 × 220 ≈ 380 V. Simply adding the two (440 V) ignores the 120° phase difference.

questions.q: While a crystalline solid is melting at its melting point, heat is still being supplied but its temperature stays constant. The heat is used to:
o: Break down the regular long-range order of the lattice
Raise the average kinetic energy of the particles
Increase the number of particles in each unit cell
questions.x: At the melting point the supplied heat (latent heat of fusion) does work against the bonding forces and breaks down the ordered lattice; the average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, does not rise until all of it has melted. Thinking the heat raises the kinetic energy contradicts the constant temperature.

questions.q: For a two-input logic gate, the output is 0 only when both inputs are 1, and 1 for every other input combination. The gate is:
questions.x: NAND is AND followed by NOT: AND gives 1 only for inputs 1, 1, so NAND gives 0 only for inputs 1, 1. AND has the opposite outputs; NOR gives 1 only for inputs 0, 0.

questions.q: A metal block gains 9 × 10⁵ J of heat energy. According to E = mc², its mass increases by: (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.x: Δm = ΔE/c² = 9 × 10⁵ / (9 × 10¹⁶) = 1 × 10⁻¹¹ kg, far too small to detect. Dividing by c instead of c² gives 3 × 10⁻³ kg; multiplying by c² gives 8.1 × 10²² kg.

questions.q: The accelerating voltage of an electron microscope is increased. Its ability to show fine detail (resolving power) improves because the electrons':
questions.x: A higher voltage gives the electrons more momentum, and λ = h/p becomes shorter; a shorter wavelength means less diffraction blurring and finer resolved detail. The electron's charge is fixed, and its mass does not fall.

questions.q: Laser light is described as coherent. This means that its waves:
o: Keep a constant phase relationship with one another
Are emitted at random times with random phases
questions.x: Coherent waves are in step: they have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, because each photon from stimulated emission is in phase with the photon that triggered it. Random phases describe ordinary (spontaneous) light.

questions.q: A GM counter placed near a radioactive source shows 50 counts per minute; with the source removed it shows a background of 10 counts per minute. With the source back in the same place, the reading after two half-lives of the source will be:
questions.x: The source alone gives 50 − 10 = 40 counts per minute, which falls to 40/4 = 10 after two half-lives; adding the unchanged background gives 10 + 10 = 20 counts per minute. Halving the total reading twice (50/4) gives 12.5; forgetting the background gives 10.

questions.q: The intensity of a beam of X-rays is halved by every 2 mm of a certain material (its half-value thickness). The fraction of the intensity that passes through 6 mm of the material is:
questions.x: 6 mm is 3 half-value thicknesses, so the intensity is halved three times: (½)³ = 1/8. Dividing by the number of thicknesses (1/3) treats the fall as linear, which is wrong for absorption.

questions.q: Which pair of atoms contains the same number of neutrons?
questions.x: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number: ¹⁴C has 14 − 6 = 8 and ¹⁶O has 16 − 8 = 8. ¹²C/¹⁴N have 6 and 7, ⁴⁰Ar/⁴⁰Ca have 22 and 20, and ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl (isotopes) have 18 and 20; equal mass number or equal atomic number is the usual mix-up.

questions.q: Iodine is extracted from its aqueous solution by shaking it with carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄ (density 1.59 g cm⁻³), in a separating funnel. After the layers settle, the iodine is mainly in the:
questions.x: CCl₄ is denser than water (1.0 g cm⁻³) and immiscible with it, so it forms the lower layer; non-polar I₂ dissolves far better in CCl₄, giving a violet colour. Taking the organic layer always to be on top (true for ether, not CCl₄) gives the upper-layer answer.

questions.q: The critical temperature of a gas is:
o: The temperature at which the gas boils at 1 atm
The temperature at which the gas becomes a plasma
The temperature above which the gas cannot be liquefied, however much pressure is applied
The temperature at which its volume becomes zero
questions.x: Above the critical temperature the molecules have too much kinetic energy for attractions to hold them as a liquid, so pressure alone cannot liquefy the gas. The boiling point at 1 atm is a lower, different temperature.

questions.q: Molecules of which compound attract each other by dipole–dipole forces?
questions.x: CHCl₃ is tetrahedral but unsymmetrical, so its bond dipoles do not cancel and it is polar. CCl₄ (tetrahedral), CO₂ (linear) and BF₃ (trigonal planar) have polar bonds whose dipoles cancel, so the molecules are non-polar.

questions.q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) describes an electron in a 3p orbital?
questions.x: A 3p electron has n = 3 and l = 1, with m = −1, 0 or +1. The set with l = 2 is a 3d electron, l = 0 is 3s, and m = −2 is impossible when l = 1.

questions.q: Which compound contains both ionic and covalent bonds in its solid, but no coordinate covalent bond?
questions.x: NaOH is Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions (ionic), and the O–H bond inside the hydroxide ion is a normal covalent bond. NH₄Cl also has ionic and covalent bonds but its NH₄⁺ ion contains a coordinate bond, so it is excluded; KCl is ionic only and HCl is covalent only.

questions.q: In the hydronium ion H₃O⁺, how many lone pairs remain on the oxygen atom, and how many of the three O–H bonds were formed as coordinate bonds?
o: Two lone pairs; one coordinate bond
One lone pair; no coordinate bond
One lone pair; one coordinate bond
No lone pair; two coordinate bonds
questions.x: Water has two lone pairs on oxygen; one of them is donated to H⁺, giving one coordinate O–H bond and leaving one lone pair (once formed, all three O–H bonds are identical). Two lone pairs is the count for H₂O itself, the most tempting slip.

questions.q: For which reaction is ΔH practically equal to ΔE (the change in internal energy)?
questions.x: ΔH = ΔE + PΔV, and for gases PΔV = ΔnRT. Only H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl has the same number of gas moles on both sides (2 → 2), so Δn = 0 and ΔH ≈ ΔE. The ammonia reaction (4 → 2) is tempting because it is so familiar, but Δn = −2.

questions.q: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) is at equilibrium in a closed vessel at constant temperature. Some CO₂ is then pumped out. What happens?
o: More CaCO₃ decomposes until the CO₂ pressure returns to its equilibrium value
CaO reacts with the remaining CO₂ to form more CaCO₃
Nothing happens, because the solids are not in the Kc expression
questions.x: Kc (or Kp) = [CO₂] only, so at a fixed temperature the CO₂ pressure must return to the same value; removing CO₂ shifts the equilibrium to the right and more CaCO₃ decomposes. The solids are absent from the expression, but that does not stop the reaction from responding.

questions.q: A 0.010 mol dm⁻³ solution of a weak acid HA has a pH of 4.0. What is Ka for HA? (ionisation is small)
questions.x: [H⁺] = [A⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, and [HA] ≈ 0.010. Ka = (1 × 10⁻⁴)² ÷ 0.010 = 1 × 10⁻⁸ ÷ 1 × 10⁻² = 1 × 10⁻⁶. 1 × 10⁻⁸ forgets to divide by the acid concentration; 1 × 10⁻⁴ is just [H⁺].

questions.q: Which salt gives a basic (alkaline) solution when dissolved in water?
questions.x: CH₃COONa is the salt of a weak acid and a strong base; the CH₃COO⁻ ion is hydrolysed, CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, so the solution is basic. NH₄Cl is acidic (weak base, strong acid), while NaCl and KNO₃ come from a strong acid and a strong base and are neutral.

questions.q: Which colligative property is most suitable for finding the molar mass of a protein or a polymer?
questions.x: For a large molecule even a few grams give very few moles, so the other effects are too small to measure, while osmotic pressure is still measurable and is taken at room temperature, where proteins are not damaged.

questions.q: When the equation MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ + H₂O is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, how many Fe²⁺ ions react with each MnO₄⁻ ion?
questions.x: Mn goes from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons; each Fe²⁺ loses 1 electron, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O (charge +17 on both sides). 8 is the coefficient of H⁺, not Fe²⁺.

questions.q: The reaction NO₂ + CO → NO + CO₂ takes place in two steps: NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO (slow), then NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂ (fast). Which rate equation does this mechanism predict?
questions.x: The slow step controls the rate, and it involves two NO₂ molecules, so rate = k[NO₂]². CO enters only after the slow step, so it does not appear. Writing the rate from the overall equation gives the tempting k[NO₂][CO].

questions.q: Calcium (atomic mass 40), strontium and barium (atomic mass 137) form one of Döbereiner's triads, in which the middle element's atomic mass is about the average of the other two. What atomic mass does this rule predict for strontium?
questions.x: Average = (40 + 137)/2 = 177/2 = 88.5, close to the real value of about 87.6. 177 is the sum without halving, and 97 is the difference.

questions.q: Which alkali metal carbonate decomposes into its oxide and carbon dioxide when heated in a Bunsen flame?
questions.x: The very small Li⁺ ion polarises the carbonate ion, so Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂ on heating, like MgCO₃ (a diagonal likeness). The other alkali metal carbonates are stable at Bunsen temperatures.

questions.q: In making silicone oils, a little (CH₃)₃SiCl is mixed with (CH₃)₂SiCl₂ before hydrolysis. The role of the (CH₃)₃SiCl is to:
o: Form cross-links between chains, since it has three methyl groups
Stop chain growth, since it has only one Si–Cl bond and so caps the chain ends
Act as a catalyst for the condensation
Absorb the HCl formed during hydrolysis
questions.x: (CH₃)₃SiCl hydrolyses to (CH₃)₃SiOH, which has only one OH and can condense at one end only, so it caps a chain and controls its length. Cross-linking needs three Si–Cl bonds on one silicon (CH₃SiCl₃); confusing three methyl groups with three Si–Cl bonds is the tempting slip.

questions.q: What volume of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaOH is needed to neutralise 25 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ completely to Na₂SO₄?
questions.x: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Acid = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol, so NaOH = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol, and 5.0 × 10⁻³ / 0.10 = 0.050 dm³ = 50 cm³. Treating sulphuric acid as monobasic gives 25 cm³.

questions.q: Which noble gas is mixed with oxygen for deep-sea divers to breathe, because it is much less soluble in blood than nitrogen?
questions.x: A helium–oxygen mixture is used because helium dissolves far less in blood than nitrogen, reducing the bends. Argon is used for inert atmospheres in bulbs and welding, and radon is radioactive.

questions.q: The iron ore magnetite has the formula:
questions.x: Magnetite is Fe₃O₄, a magnetic mixed oxide. Haematite is Fe₂O₃, siderite FeCO₃ and iron pyrites FeS₂; haematite is the usual mix-up.

questions.q: Which compound is a secondary alcohol?
questions.x: In butan-2-ol the carbon bearing OH is bonded to two other carbons, so it is secondary. The propanol and butan-1-ol given are primary (one C attached), and (CH₃)₃COH is tertiary (three C attached).

questions.q: 5.6 g of an open-chain alkene reacts completely with exactly 16.0 g of bromine (Br = 80). Whichever way HBr adds across its double bond, the alkene can give only one structural product. The alkene is:
questions.x: 16.0 g Br₂ = 0.10 mol, so the alkene's molar mass is 56 g mol⁻¹: C₄H₈. But-2-ene is symmetrical and gives only 2-bromobutane; but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene can each give two bromides. Propene (42) is ruled out by the mass; taking Br₂ as 80 instead of 160 gives an impossible 28 g mol⁻¹.

questions.q: Which statement about the two Kekulé structures of benzene is correct?
o: The molecule switches rapidly back and forth between the two structures
Half of all benzene molecules have one structure and half have the other
The two structures differ in the positions of the carbon atoms
The real molecule is a single resonance hybrid, and neither Kekulé structure exists on its own
questions.x: Resonance structures differ only in where the electrons are drawn; the atoms stay put. Benzene is one hybrid with all bonds equal; 'rapid switching' is the common misreading of the resonance arrow ↔ as an equilibrium ⇌.

questions.q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CHClCH(CH₃)₂ is:
questions.x: The longest chain has 4 carbons. Numbering from either end puts the substituents at 2 and 3, so the tie is broken alphabetically: chloro comes before methyl and gets the lower number. 3-Chloro-2-methylbutane numbers from the wrong end; '2-methyl-3-chloro' breaks the alphabetical order.

questions.q: Ethanol is warmed with ethanoic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid. The sweet-smelling product is:
questions.x: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid give an ester and water (esterification): CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, with H₂SO₄ as catalyst. Ethoxyethane and ethene form from ethanol and H₂SO₄ alone, without the acid.

questions.q: In the aldol condensation of ethanal with dilute NaOH, the species that attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal molecule is:
o: ⁻CH₂CHO, formed when OH⁻ removes an α-hydrogen
H⁻, transferred from another ethanal molecule
questions.x: OH⁻ acts as a base and takes an H from the CH₃ next to the C=O; the carbanion (enolate) is the nucleophile. Hydride transfer is the key step of the Cannizzaro reaction, which needs an aldehyde without α-hydrogens.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of alanine, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH, is:
questions.x: The chain has three carbons including the COOH carbon, which is C-1, so NH₂ on the next carbon is at C-2: 2-aminopropanoic acid. Numbering from the CH₃ end gives 3-amino, and 2-aminoethanoic acid is glycine.

questions.q: Benzenediazonium chloride, made below 5 °C, is added to a cold alkaline solution of phenol. The product is:
questions.x: This is a coupling reaction: the diazonium ion attacks the phenol ring (mainly at the 4-position) and the –N=N– link is kept, giving a coloured azo dye. Phenol and N₂ form when the diazonium salt is warmed in water, which is a different reaction.

questions.q: A compound C₄H₈O₂ shows three ¹H NMR signals: a triplet (3H) at δ 1.3, a singlet (3H) at δ 2.0 and a quartet (2H) at δ 4.1. Protons on a carbon bonded directly to an ester oxygen appear near δ 3.5–4.5; those on a carbon next to C=O near δ 2.0–2.5. The compound is:
questions.x: Triplet plus quartet shows an ethyl group, and the quartet at δ 4.1 puts its CH₂ on the ester oxygen; the singlet at δ 2.0 is a CH₃ next to C=O: ethyl ethanoate. Methyl propanoate also gives a triplet, quartet and singlet, but its quartet would be near δ 2.3 and its singlet near δ 3.7.

questions.q: 10 000 dm³ of acid rain of pH 4.0 drains into a pond. What mass of powdered limestone, CaCO₃ (100 g mol⁻¹), is needed to neutralise its H⁺ ions? (CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O)
questions.x: pH 4.0 means [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, so H⁺ = 10 000 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.0 mol. This needs 0.50 mol CaCO₃ = 50 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio instead of 1 : 2 gives 100 g.

questions.q: Which of the following tasks is NOT done by the control unit?
o: Directing data between the CPU parts
questions.x: Arithmetic such as adding is carried out by the ALU. The control unit decodes instructions, sends control and timing signals and directs the flow of data, but it does not do the calculation itself.

questions.q: An 8-bit data bus is used to bring a 32-bit number from memory. What is the smallest number of transfers needed?
questions.x: Each transfer carries 8 bits, so 32 ÷ 8 = 4 transfers are needed. One transfer would only be enough if the bus were 32 bits wide.

questions.q: At a shop counter, the cashier passes each packet over a device that reads the black-and-white stripes printed on it. Which input device is this?
questions.x: A barcode reader shines light on the printed bars and reads the product code from them. An optical mark reader senses filled-in circles on answer sheets, not product stripes.

questions.q: Two star networks each have 5 computers, every computer joined by its own cable to that network's switch. The two switches are then joined by one cable. How many cables are used in total?
questions.x: Each star needs 5 cables, giving 5 + 5 = 10, and one more cable joins the two switches: 10 + 1 = 11. 10 forgets the cable between the switches.

questions.q: At the receiving end of a telephone-line connection, a modem changes the analogue signal back into digital data. This step is called:
questions.x: Turning the received analogue signal back into digital data is demodulation, the 'dem' part of modem. Modulation is the opposite step, done at the sending end.

questions.q: Which device connects two networks that use different protocols, translating between them?
questions.x: A gateway converts data from one protocol to another so that dissimilar networks can communicate. A repeater only boosts signals, and a hub only copies them to all ports.

questions.q: Which statement is true of a computer virus but NOT of a worm?
o: It is a type of malware
It can damage or delete data
It can spread from one computer to another
It must attach itself to a host file or program to spread
questions.x: A virus needs a host file or program to travel in, while a worm copies itself on its own across a network. Being malware, damaging data and spreading between computers are true of both.

questions.q: Software that may be used free of charge for as long as one likes, while its author keeps the copyright and does not share the source code, is called:
questions.x: Freeware is free to use with no time limit, but it stays copyrighted and closed. Shareware is free only for a trial, open-source shares its code, and public domain work has no copyright.

questions.q: A school designs its newsletter on a computer, arranging text, headings and photos on each page before printing. This is:
questions.x: Desktop publishing (DTP) is the page layout of text and pictures for documents such as newsletters and brochures. CAM controls machines in a factory.

questions.q: A long table runs over 3 pages, and its heading row must appear at the top of the table on every page. Which feature does this?
questions.x: Repeat Header Rows makes the chosen top row appear again wherever the table continues on a new page. Split Table would break the table into two separate tables.

questions.q: Which feature shows how the pages of a document will look on paper, before it is actually printed?
questions.x: Print Preview displays the pages as they will be printed, so layout problems can be fixed first. Format Painter copies formatting from one piece of text to another.

questions.q: Teacher(TeacherID, Name, DeptID) has DeptID as a foreign key to Dept, with referential integrity enforced. DeptID is not set as required. A new teacher is added with DeptID left empty (NULL) because the department is not decided yet. What happens?
o: It is allowed, because a foreign key may be NULL unless it is made required
It is refused, because a foreign key can never be NULL
It is refused, because it breaks entity integrity
It is allowed only if DeptID is the primary key of Teacher
questions.x: Referential integrity says a non-empty foreign key must match a primary key value; an empty (NULL) value matches nothing and is allowed unless the field is required. Entity integrity applies to the primary key TeacherID, not to DeptID.

questions.q: A file must use direct (random) organisation so that any record can be reached at once without reading the others. On which storage medium can it be kept?
o: A reel of punched paper tape
questions.x: A disk's read/write head can move straight to any address, so direct files are kept on disks. Tape must be wound past every earlier record, so it allows sequential access only.

questions.q: Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptHead) has the key EmpID, with EmpID → Name, EmpID → DeptID and DeptID → DeptHead. Which split puts it into 3NF without losing any information?
o: Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptHead) and Dept(DeptID, DeptHead)
Emp(EmpID, Name, DeptID) and Dept(DeptID, DeptHead)
questions.x: The transitive part DeptID → DeptHead moves to its own table, and DeptID stays in Emp as a foreign key to link the two. Without DeptID in Emp there is no way to know which department an employee is in.

questions.q: Which form control shows the value of a field and lets the user type or change it?
questions.x: A bound text box displays a field's value and accepts typing. A label only shows fixed text, such as a heading or a field's caption.

questions.q: Which view shows how a report will look on paper, page by page, before it is printed?
questions.x: Print Preview shows the finished pages as they will print. Design View shows the sections and controls for editing the layout, not the final pages.

questions.q: In `char name[20]; scanf("%s", name);` why is no & written before name?
o: Strings can be read only from files, not from the keyboard
The & sign is needed only with printf
scanf first reads the string into a temporary variable
The name of an array already gives the address of the array
questions.x: scanf needs addresses, and an array's name stands for the address of its first element, so name is already an address. For a plain int variable the & is needed to give its address.
x *= 2 + 3 means x = x * (2 + 3), because the whole right side is worked out first: 4 × 5 = 20. Reading it as x * 2 + 3 gives the tempting 11.

o: The compiler reports an error, because `k` is not visible at the `printf`
questions.x: k is a local variable of the inner block { }, so it exists only inside that block; using it in the printf after the block is a compile error. Inside the block t was changed to 7, but the program never runs.
n > 0 is false, so its value is 0 and control jumps to case 0, printing not positive; break ends the switch. A relational expression is a normal int (0 or 1), so it can be the switch expression.
Odd i is added and even i is subtracted: 1 - 2 + 3 - 4 + 5 - 6 = -3. 21 adds all six numbers and 9 adds only the odd ones.

questions.q: A project's cost estimate is Rs 800,000. The plan adds a contingency reserve of 15% of this amount for risks. What total budget should be requested?

The programmer wanted this Python code to print the numbers 1 to 5. What is wrong with it?
```
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
```
o: A syntax error: the condition of `while` needs brackets
A logic error: `i` never changes, so 1 is printed again and again without end
A runtime error on the first line
questions.x: The line i = i + 1 is missing, so i stays 1, i <= 5 is always true and the loop never ends. The code is valid Python (brackets round the condition are optional), so it is a logic error, not a syntax error.

questions.q: Which of these values has the data type `float`?
questions.x: A number written with a decimal point, `5.0`, is a float. `"5.0"` is in quotes, so it is a string; `5` is an int and `True` is a bool.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
count = 0
for n in [3, 8, 12, 5, 6]:
    if n % 3 == 0:
        count += 1
print(count)
```
questions.x: Only 3, 12 and 6 leave remainder 0 when divided by 3, so `count` becomes 3. 21 is their sum, but the loop adds 1 each time, not the number.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
s = "MULTAN"
print(s[2:] + s[:2])
```
questions.x: `s[2:]` runs from index 2 (L) to the end: "LTAN". `s[:2]` is indexes 0 and 1: "MU", because the end index is excluded. Joined: LTANMU. LTANMUL wrongly includes index 2 in `s[:2]`.

questions.q:
For a large `n`, how does the number of passes of this loop grow?
```
i = 1
while i < n:
    i = i * 2
```
questions.x: i doubles each pass (1, 2, 4, 8, …), so it reaches n after about log₂ n passes: O(log n). It would be O(n) only if i went up by 1 each pass.

questions.q: Binary search looks for 12 in `[5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35]` (indexes 0 to 6), using middle index = (low + high) // 2 and stopping when low > high. Which values are compared with 12, in order?
questions.x: mid = 3 (20): 12 < 20, high = 2. mid = 1 (10): 12 > 10, low = 2. mid = 2 (15): 12 < 15, high = 1. Now low > high, so 12 is not found after comparing 20, 10, 15. Stopping after 10 misses the last check.

questions.q: When is p ∧ q true?
o: When p and q are both true
When at least one of p and q is true
When p and q have the same truth value
When p is true and q is false
questions.x: A conjunction is true only when both parts are true. "At least one true" describes p ∨ q, and "same truth value" describes p ↔ q.

questions.q: An online shop sells 150 shirts a month at Rs 800 each. Each shirt costs Rs 500 to make, and the shop's fixed costs are Rs 30,000 a month. What is its monthly profit?
questions.x: Each shirt earns 800 − 500 = Rs 300 over its cost, so 150 × 300 = Rs 45,000; minus fixed costs of Rs 30,000 leaves Rs 15,000 profit. Rs 45,000 forgets the fixed costs, and Rs 120,000 is the sales revenue.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
o: The narrator's bicycle was stolen and later found by his grandfather
A small weekly habit, begun with a simple gift, proved more valuable than it first seemed
Children should never shake their money boxes
The narrator persuaded his parents to buy him a new bicycle
questions.x: The narrator first thought the pot "a dull present" but later realised "He had given me a habit". He did not ask his parents: "I was too proud to ask".

questions.q: What did the narrator buy with the money from the pot?
o: A second-hand bicycle and a lock
questions.x: The pot held "enough for a second-hand bicycle and a lock". The bicycle was second-hand, not new.

questions.q: The stopping of the rattle mattered to the narrator because it:
o: meant that the pot had cracked and had to be broken
told him exactly how much money he had saved
showed that his small coins had added up, which encouraged him to save more
made him decide to break the pot at once
questions.x: The silence meant "the pot was too full for the coins to move"; after that "something shifted" and he began adding notes "every Friday". It could not tell him the exact total, and he broke the pot only years later.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "fed" most nearly means:
questions.x: He "fed it only when I remembered", meaning he dropped coins into the pot. Giving food is the word's usual meaning, which a clay pot cannot take.

questions.q: In the last paragraph, the narrator's attitude towards his grandfather's gift is best described as:
o: resentful, wishing it had been money
amused, treating it as a joke
questions.x: He realises the gift was "a habit, and the pot was only the excuse", which shows appreciation. Finding it dull was his feeling at eleven, in the second paragraph, not at the end.

questions.q: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
o: Loud coaches teach young players more than quiet ones
A coach taught most effectively by letting the narrator discover a lesson himself
Keeping the head still is the most important skill in bowling
The narrator nearly left the club because of an unfriendly coach
questions.x: The lessons "that stayed with me were the ones Master Yousaf let me find for myself". The narrator says he learned from louder coaches "too", but less lastingly, so they did not teach him more.

questions.q: What did the narrator discover during the practice with the cup?
o: The cup had been placed too far away to be hit
His good deliveries came when he kept his head still as he let go of the ball
Most of his good balls went down the leg side
He bowled better when the coach stood close by
questions.x: He noticed that "the good ones came when I kept my head still at the moment of release". It was most of his poor balls, not the good ones, that "sprayed down the leg side".

questions.q: The narrator's belief after the first evening that the coach had "already written me off" proved to be:
o: correct, since the coach never gave him any help
correct, because the coach preferred louder players
wrong, as the coach's later attention showed
wrong, because the coach praised him that same evening
questions.x: The next week the coach set him a task, smiled at his discovery and said "Good", so he had not given up on him. The coach did not praise him on the first evening; he only "nodded, and walked away".

questions.q: As used in the first paragraph, the phrase "written me off" most nearly means:
o: put my name on the team list
sent me a letter of refusal
decided I was not worth bothering with
questions.x: After the coach "nodded, and walked away", the narrator feared he had been judged worthless, which is what "written me off" means. Nothing was literally written, so the letter and the paper notes are wrong.

questions.q: Looking back as an adult, how does the narrator regard Master Yousaf's silence?
o: He resents it as a lack of interest in young players
He values it as a wise way of teaching and tries to copy it
He finds it amusing but of little real use
He regrets that it kept him from learning more
questions.x: He calls it "his patient silence" and, when coaching boys of his own, says "I remember that cup, and I keep quiet a little longer". Resentment is wrong: the lessons it gave are the ones that "stayed with me".
